The optional `--exclude_cis_omega` flag filters out structures with **cis peptide bonds**, which are rare in natural proteins (< 0.1% of non-proline peptide bonds). The filter operates on the dequantized omega dihedral angle before full reconstruction: structures are retained only if **all** omega angles in the fragment satisfy `|ω| > 90°` (i.e., all peptide bonds are in the trans conformation). This filter is applied inside `extract_data` at the raw angle level, avoiding the computational cost of full coordinate reconstruction for structures that would be discarded.

Sources: [extract_structures_from_foldcomp_database.py](/scripts/extract_structures_from_foldcomp_database.py#L230-L235)

## Orchestration — `compute_ensembles` and `extract_data`

The top-level `compute_ensembles` function drives the full per-fragment pipeline. For each fragment key in the search results dictionary, it: (1) reads the fragment ensemble from the Foldcomp database via `extract_data`, which iterates over all hits `(fasta_byte_start, byte_start, aa_start_index)` and loads reconstruction data for the residue range `[l, l+nres)`, stacking results via `join_list_of_identical_pytrees`; (2) subsamples if the number of structures exceeds `n_max_structures_per_fragment` using random index selection; (3) reconstructs the full ensemble in one batched call via the JIT-compiled `build_parallel_reconstruct_fn`; and (4) converts the coordinates from Ångströms to nanometers (÷10.0) and saves the trajectory as an HDF5 file using mdtraj, with topology built from the fragment sequence via `build_mdtraj_top`.

| Step | Function | Key Operation |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `extract_data` | Load & stack reconstruction data from all hits |
| 2 | Random subsampling | Cap to `n_max_structures_per_fragment` |
| 3 | `build_parallel_reconstruct_fn` → `jit_fn(...)` | Batch-reconstruct all structures |
| 4 | `md.Trajectory(...)` + `.save_hdf5(...)` | Serialize to HDF5 with mdtraj topology |

Sources: [extract_structures_from_foldcomp_database.py](/scripts/extract_structures_from_foldcomp_database.py#L217-L268)

## CLI Interface

The script is invoked as a standalone command after the search stage has produced `byte_starts.pkl`:

```bash
python3 scripts/extract_structures_from_foldcomp_database.py \
  --byte_starts_path /tmp/byte_starts.pkl \
  --foldcomp_fasta /data/afdb_uniprot_v4.fasta \
  --foldcomp_db /data/afdb_uniprot_v4 \
  --outfolder /tmp/fragment_ensembles \
  --n_max_structures_per_fragment 1000 \
  --exclude_cis_omega
```

| Argument | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `--byte_starts_path` | (required) | Pickle file from search stage with hit metadata |
| `--foldcomp_fasta` | `/data/afdb_uniprot_v4.fasta` | Offset-annotated FASTA for the Foldcomp database |
| `--foldcomp_db` | `/data/afdb_uniprot_v4` | Path to the binary Foldcomp database file |
| `--outfolder` | (required) | Output directory for per-fragment `.h5` ensemble files |
| `--n_max_structures_per_fragment` | `1000` | Maximum structures to extract per fragment |
| `--exclude_cis_omega` | `False` | Exclude structures with cis peptide bonds |

When invoked through `build_ensemble.py`, these arguments are populated automatically from the ensemble builder's CLI arguments, and the stage runs as the second step between `fasta_search_in_foldcomp_database.main()` and `join_fragments.main()`.

Sources: [extract_structures_from_foldcomp_database.py](/scripts/extract_structures_from_foldcomp_database.py#L277-L326), [build_ensemble.py](/scripts/build_ensemble.py#L60-L70)

## Data Flow Across Pipeline Stages

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Search ["Stage 1: Sequence Search"]
        S1["foldcomp.fasta"] --> S2["byte_starts.pkl"]
    end
    subgraph Reconstruct ["Stage 2: Structure Reconstruction"]
        R1["byte_starts.pkl"] --> R2["Foldcomp DB<br/>[binary]"]
        R2 --> R3["Fragment Ensembles<br/>(.h5 per fragment)"]
    end
    subgraph Join ["Stage 3: Fragment Joining"]
        J1["Fragment Ensembles"] --> J2["Full-chain Ensemble<br/>(.h5/.xtc/.pdb)"]
    end

    S2 --> R1
    R3 --> J1

    style Reconstruct fill:#2d3748,color:#fff
```

The reconstruction stage consumes the `byte_starts.pkl` pickle file produced by [GPU-Accelerated Sequence Search](6-gpu-accelerated-sequence-search), which maps each fragment sequence to a tuple of three arrays: `hit_idxs` (byte positions in the FASTA file), `byte_starts` (byte positions in the Foldcomp database), and `aa_start_index` (residue offset within the matched entry). It produces one `.h5` file per fragment containing an mdtraj-compatible trajectory of all reconstructed conformations, which is then consumed by [Hierarchical Fragment Joining](8-hierarchical-fragment-joining).

> [!TIP]
> The `join_list_of_identical_pytrees` utility function uses JAX's pytree flattening/unflattening to stack heterogeneous reconstruction data tuples across multiple hits into batched arrays. This enables the subsequent single-call batched JIT reconstruction, which is far more efficient than per-structure reconstruction loops.

Sources: [extract_structures_from_foldcomp_database.py](/scripts/extract_structures_from_foldcomp_database.py#L209-L214), [extract_structures_from_foldcomp_database.py](/scripts/extract_structures_from_foldcomp_database.py#L240-L268)

## Next Steps

With fragment ensembles reconstructed and saved as `.h5` files, the pipeline proceeds to [Hierarchical Fragment Joining](8-hierarchical-fragment-joining), where overlapping fragment pairs are aligned on their shared residues, validated for steric clashes, and progressively merged into a complete-chain ensemble. For the full end-to-end invocation, see [Quick Start](2-quick-start); for parameter tuning of the reconstruction stage specifically, consult [Command-Line Configuration Reference](13-command-line-configuration-reference).

# Hierarchical Fragment Joining



The hierarchical fragment joining stage is the combinatorial core of the IDP-o pipeline — it transforms per-fragment structural ensembles (reconstructed from Foldcomp) into a globally consistent ensemble for the full target sequence. Rather than joining fragments linearly from left to right, the system decomposes the fragment list into **power-of-two segments**, joins each segment via a **balanced binary tree**, then **linearly combines** the resulting super-fragments. This hierarchy minimizes the accumulation of alignment error and distributes clash probability more evenly across the join graph, producing ensembles with superior structural coherence compared to naïve sequential joining.

## From Fragments to Full Sequence

The joining process operates on the output of the fragment generation strategy, which partitions a target sequence of length *L* into overlapping fragments of `seq_len=6` residues with an `overlap=2` residue window. With a stride of 4 (`seq_len - overlap`), a sequence of length *L* yields approximately ⌈(*L* − 4) / 4⌉ + 1 fragments. Each fragment carries an ensemble of conformations (coordinates, backbone indices, and uniform or derived probability weights) loaded from per-fragment `.h5` files produced by [Structure Reconstruction from Foldcomp](7-structure-reconstruction-from-foldcomp).

The `generate_fragments` function implements this partitioning: it shifts a sliding window by `seq_len - overlap` residues at each step, ensuring every adjacent pair shares exactly 2 residues in common — the **join interface** upon which structural alignment is performed. A degenerate trailing fragment of length equal to the overlap is discarded, since it carries no new structural information.

Sources: [fasta_search_in_foldcomp_database.py](/scripts/fasta_search_in_foldcomp_database.py#L147-L152), [join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L286-L288)

## The Pairwise Join: Alignment, Validation, and Acceptance

At the atomic level, every join in the hierarchy is a **pairwise operation** combining a left fragment *l* and a right fragment *r* that share a 2-residue overlap. The `join_fragments` function orchestrates this as a Monte Carlo-style sampling procedure:

1. **Weighted conformation sampling** — `n` conformation indices are drawn independently from each fragment's ensemble according to their probability distributions (`lprobs`, `rprobs`), producing `n` candidate left-right pairs.
2. **Vectorized alignment and validation** — for each pair, the right fragment is superimposed onto the left via the overlap backbone atoms, then the merged structure is checked for steric clashes.
3. **Filtering** — only pairs satisfying both an **RMSD threshold** (< 0.06 nm = 0.6 Å on the overlap backbone) and a **clash-free condition** survive the filter mask.
4. **Retry with resampling** — if no valid pairs are found, new random indices are drawn up to 5 attempts before falling back to a single random selection.

The number of samples `n` is rounded up to a multiple of the chunk size, which is itself computed from a memory-budget heuristic: `batch_size = target_GB / (1e-5 × nres²)`, where `nres` is the total number of residues in the joined sequence. This ensures GPU memory utilization stays within the 96% XLA allocation cap set at module import.

Sources: [join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L147-L192)

### Overlap Alignment via SVD

The alignment of the right fragment onto the left is performed by `affine_alignment`, which computes the **optimal rigid-body transformation** (rotation + translation) minimizing RMSD between the two overlap regions. This is the classical Kabsch algorithm implemented in JAX:

- **Center** both coordinate sets by subtracting their centroids.
- **Compute** the cross-covariance matrix *R* = (*x* − *x̄*)<sup>T</sup>(*y* − *ȳ*).
- **Decompose** *R* via SVD: *R* = *USV*<sup>T</sup>.
- **Correct** for reflection: if det(*UV*<sup>T</sup>) < 0, flip the sign of the last row of *V*<sup>T</sup>.
- **Compose** the rotation *Q* = *UV*<sup>T</sup>.

The `align` function then applies this transformation to the entire mobile (right) coordinate set, not just the overlap — this is what positions the non-overlapping portion of the right fragment correctly in the merged frame.

Sources: [join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L38-L57)

### Clash Detection

After alignment, the merged coordinate array is tested by `check_interactions`, which computes the full pairwise distance matrix and flags any non-bonded atom pair closer than `cutoff=0.1` nm (1.0 Å). Bonded pairs (from the mdtraj topology) are excluded from the check. The function returns a boolean mask over upper-triangular pairs, and `_join_fragments` reduces this to a single `no_clash_mask = ~mask.any()` per candidate. This extremely tight cutoff filters out only the most severe steric violations — appropriate for the intrinsically disordered context where moderate van der Waals overlap is expected and tolerable.

Sources: [join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L60-L69), [join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L112-L123)

### The Core Join Kernel

The `_join_fragments` function is the JAX-compiled inner loop that processes a single pair of sampled conformations. Its logic is:

- Extract the **overlap backbone atom indices** from each fragment: for the left fragment, the last `overlap=2` residues supply their `(C, O)` atoms; for the right, the first 2 residues supply `(N, CA)`. These four atoms per side (8 total) form the peptide bond join interface.
- **Vectorize** over the batch via `vmap(align_and_validate)`, producing aligned positions, clash masks, and RMSDs for all `n` candidates simultaneously.
- **Combine** the quality criteria: `mask = (rmsds < 0.06) & no_clash_mask`.

The `static_context` tuple `(lhs, rhs)` marks the atom index boundary between the left and right fragments in the merged coordinate array — `lhs` is the first atom index after the left fragment's contribution, `rhs` is the first atom index of the right fragment's non-overlap region. The merged position array is constructed as `concat([lpos[:lhs], rpos_aligned[rhs:]])`, discarding the redundant overlap coordinates from the right fragment.

Sources: [join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L96-L123)

## Hierarchical Joining Strategy

The `build_ensemble` function implements the **hierarchical decomposition** that distinguishes IDP-o's joining from simple left-to-right accumulation. The algorithm proceeds in two phases:

**Phase 1 — Power-of-two binary tree joins.** The fragment count *N* is decomposed into its binary representation (up to 16 bits). Each set bit at position *k* produces a segment of 2<sup>*k*</sup> fragments. Within each segment, joining proceeds in ⌊log₂(segment_size)⌋ rounds: in round *i*, adjacent pairs from round *i*−1 are joined pairwise, halving the number of super-fragments each round until a single super-fragment remains. Smaller segments are joined first (the `segments[::-1]` reversal), which ensures that the join tree is balanced within each power-of-two block.

**Phase 2 — Linear combination of super-fragments.** The super-fragments from each power-of-two segment are joined sequentially from left to right. This phase is only needed when *N* is not itself a power of two.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "Phase 1: Binary Tree (example: N=6 → 4+2)"
        direction TB
        F1["f₁"] --> J12["Join"]
        F2["f₂"] --> J12
        F3["f₃"] --> J34["Join"]
        F4["f₄"] --> J34
        J12 --> J1234["Join"]
        J34 --> J1234
        F5["f₅"] --> J56["Join"]
        F6["f₆"] --> J56
    end
    subgraph "Phase 2: Linear Combine"
        J1234 --> Jfinal["Join"]
        J56 --> Jfinal
    end
    Jfinal --> Full["Full Sequence Ensemble"]
```

For the example above with 6 fragments, the 4-fragment segment is joined in a balanced tree (2 rounds), the 2-fragment segment in one round, and the two resulting super-fragments are combined linearly.

> [!TIP]
> The binary decomposition ensures that the maximum depth of any join chain is ⌊log₂(N)⌋ + (number_of_set_bits − 1), compared to N−1 for naïve linear joining. This dramatically reduces cumulative alignment error propagation.

Sources: [join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L195-L249)

### Probability Propagation

After each successful join, the resulting super-fragment is stored in the shared `data` dictionary with **product probabilities** derived from the source conformation indices. The `get_probs` function computes the inverse-frequency weight for each unique conformation index in the source array (implementing importance weighting for non-uniform fragment ensembles), and the joined ensemble's probability is the element-wise product of the left and right source probabilities via `jax.tree.map(jnp.multiply, ...)`. This ensures that conformations drawn from high-probability regions of both fragments are favored in the joined ensemble.

Sources: [join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L126-L129), [join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L218-L223)

### Memory Management

GPU device memory is reclaimed aggressively between hierarchy levels. Once a join round completes (when `i > 1`), all `jax.Array` objects from two levels prior are explicitly deleted via `.delete()`. This is critical because the coordinate arrays for intermediate super-fragments grow proportionally to the number of residues, and without cleanup the device would exhaust its 96% allocation well before the final join. The XLA backend's `live_buffers()` are also purged at the start of the `main` function before any joining begins.

Sources: [join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L228-L234), [join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L289-L292)

## JAX Vectorization and Chunked Execution

The `jit_chunked_vmap` function is the bridge between JAX's compile-time vectorization and runtime memory constraints. Rather than applying `vmap` across the full batch of `n` candidates (which would materialize an *n × n_atoms × 3* coordinate tensor and an *n × n_atoms × n_atoms* distance tensor simultaneously), it reshapes the input arrays into chunks of `chunk_size`, then uses `jax.lax.scan` to iterate over chunks sequentially within a single compiled computation. This preserves the performance benefits of XLA optimization within each chunk while keeping peak memory bounded by the chunk size rather than the total batch size.

The chunk size is determined by the `batch_size` lambda, which targets approximately 10 GB of device memory and scales inversely with the square of the residue count (reflecting the *O(n²)* cost of the pairwise distance computation in `check_interactions`).

Sources: [join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L132-L144), [join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L150-L151)

## Post-Join Processing: RMSD Sorting and Hydrogen Insertion

After the full ensemble is assembled, two optional transformations are applied:

1. **RMSD-based trajectory sorting** — when `--rmsd_sort` is enabled, `sort_trajectory` superposes all frames to frame 0, computes the full RMSD matrix, then orders frames by greedy nearest-neighbor in RMSD space. This produces a trajectory that varies smoothly frame-to-frame, which is essential for visual inspection in molecular viewers.

2. **Hydrogen atom insertion** — the `infer_and_insert_hydrogens` function from `nerfax.reduce_utils` reconstructs hydrogen atom positions from the heavy-atom backbone and sidechain coordinates, producing a complete all-atom trajectory suitable for downstream MD or analysis workflows.

Sources: [join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L252-L274), [join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L308-L319)

## Command-Line Interface

The `join_fragments.py` script exposes the following arguments for controlling the joining process:

| Argument | Type | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--sequence` | str | *(required)* | Target amino acid sequence |
| `--fragments_folder` | str | *(required)* | Path to per-fragment `.h5` ensemble files |
| `--outpath` | str | *(required)* | Output trajectory path (`.h5`, `.xtc`, `.dcd`, `.pdb`) |
| `--joins_to_attempt_per_pairing` | int | 500000 | Number of candidate conformation pairs to sample per join |
| `--max_structures_in_ensemble` | int | 500000 | Maximum number of conformations in the final output ensemble |
| `--rmsd_sort` | flag | False | Sort trajectory by RMSD for smooth visualization |
| `--overwrite` | flag | False | Overwrite existing output file |

Note that `join_fragments.py` is typically invoked indirectly through `build_ensemble.py`, which orchestrates the full pipeline (search → extract → join). The standalone invocation is useful when fragment ensembles have already been extracted and only the joining step needs to be rerun or tuned.

Sources: [join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L323-L347), [build_ensemble.py](/scripts/build_ensemble.py#L71-L80)

## Architectural Summary

The following table summarizes the key computational components and their roles within the hierarchical joining stage:

| Component | Role | Complexity Class |
|---|---|---|
| `affine_alignment` | Optimal rigid-body superposition via SVD | *O(n)* per alignment |
| `align` | Apply rotation/translation to full mobile coords | *O(n)* per alignment |
| `check_interactions` | Pairwise steric clash detection | *O(n²)* per candidate |
| `_join_fragments` | Vectorized align + validate + filter | *O(batch × n²)* |
| `jit_chunked_vmap` | Memory-batched XLA-compiled scan | *O((n/chunks) × chunk × n²)* |
| `join_fragments` | Sample, join, retry loop for one pair | *O(attempts × n_joins × nres²)* |
| `build_ensemble` | Hierarchical tree + linear combine | *O(log N)* depth of joins |

> [!TIP]
> The 2-residue overlap is hardcoded throughout the pipeline (`overlap = 2` in both `pre_join_fragments` and `_join_fragments`). Modifying this value requires coordinated changes to `generate_fragments`, the backbone index extraction logic, and the overlap atom selection in `_join_fragments` — it is not a simple parameter change.

The hierarchical fragment joining stage produces the complete conformational ensemble that feeds into [JAX Vectorized Ensemble Computation](10-jax-vectorized-ensemble-computation) for downstream analysis. For a deeper treatment of the alignment mathematics and clash criteria, see [Overlap Alignment and Clash Detection](9-overlap-alignment-and-clash-detection). To understand how this stage fits into the full pipeline orchestration, consult [Architecture Overview](4-architecture-overview).

# Overlap Alignment and Clash Detection



When two structural fragments share a common residue sequence, their 3D coordinates almost never agree — the fragments originate from different database entries with different backbone conformations. The **overlap alignment** algorithm resolves this by computing the rigid-body transformation that best superimposes the shared backbone atoms, while **clash detection** rejects any resulting conformation where non-bonded atoms are driven into physically impossible proximity. Together, these two gates form the quality filter at the core of IDP-o's fragment joining pipeline, deciding which candidate joins survive into the final ensemble.

## The Overlap Region: Peptide-Bond Anchoring

IDP-o fragments each have a length of 6 residues with a **2-residue overlap** between adjacent fragments. This overlap is not arbitrary — it provides just enough backbone atoms to uniquely determine the relative orientation of two fragments. The `generate_fragments` function produces fragments by shifting a window of `seq_len=6` along the sequence with a stride of `seq_len - overlap = 4`, so that each pair of consecutive fragments shares residues at positions `[i-2, i-1]` and `[i-2, i-1]` respectively.

```python
fragments = [s[i * shift : i * shift + seq_len] for i in range((len(s) - seq_len) // shift + 2)]
```

The assertion `l[-overlap:] == r[:overlap]` in `pre_join_fragments` guarantees that the overlapping residues match at the sequence level before any structural comparison is attempted. The merged sequence is then constructed as `l + r[overlap:]`, avoiding duplication of the shared residues.

Sources: [fasta_search_in_foldcomp_database.py](scripts/fasta_search_in_foldcomp_database.py#L146-L150), [join_fragments.py](scripts/join_fragments.py#L88-L93)

## Selecting Alignment Anchor Atoms

Rather than aligning on all 8 backbone atoms (N, CA, C, O × 2 residues) in the overlap, IDP-o selects a **4-atom subset** that straddles the peptide bond between the two overlap residues:

| Fragment | Overlap Residues | `.ravel()` (8 atoms) | `[2:-2]` slice (4 atoms) |
|----------|-----------------|----------------------|---------------------------|
| Left (last 2 residues) | i−1, i | N,CA,C,O,N,CA,C,O | **C**₍ᵢ₋₁₎, **O**₍ᵢ₋₁₎, **N**₍ᵢ₎, **CA**₍ᵢ₎ |
| Right (first 2 residues) | i−1, i | N,CA,C,O,N,CA,C,O | **C**₍ᵢ₋₁₎, **O**₍ᵢ₋₁₎, **N**₍ᵢ₎, **CA**₍ᵢ₎ |

```python
l_indices, r_indices = (
    bb_indices[indexing].ravel()[2:-2]  # (C, O)_i, (N, CA)_(iplus1), join on peptide bond
    for bb_indices, indexing in [
        (l_bb_indices, jnp.arange(-overlap, 0)),
        (r_bb_indices, jnp.arange(overlap)),
    ]
)
```

This is a deliberate design choice: the C–N peptide bond is the most geometrically constrained feature of the polypeptide backbone (partial double-bond character restricts rotation around it). By anchoring the alignment on the atoms flanking this bond — C and O of the upstream residue, N and CA of the downstream residue — the algorithm targets the most physically informative reference frame. Dropping the outer atoms (N, CA of the upstream residue and C, O of the downstream residue) avoids diluting the alignment signal with atoms that are more conformationally variable.

> [!TIP]
> The `[2:-2]` slice is not trimming outliers — it is extracting the 4 atoms that physically define the peptide-bond junction. This is why the overlap must be exactly 2 residues: fewer residues would not provide enough backbone atoms to anchor the alignment.

Sources: [join_fragments.py](scripts/join_fragments.py#L106-L115)

## Kabsch Alignment: The Affine Registration

The `affine_alignment` function implements the **Kabsch algorithm** — the closed-form solution for the optimal rotation matrix that minimizes the RMSD between two paired point sets. Given a mobile point set **P** and a reference point set **Q**, the algorithm proceeds in three stages:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Center both point sets<br/>P̄ = P − mean(P)<br/>Q̄ = Q − mean(Q)"] --> B["Compute cross-covariance<br/>R = P̄ᵀ · Q̄"]
    B --> C["Singular Value Decomposition<br/>R = U · S · Vᵀ"]
    C --> D{"det(U · Vᵀ) < 0?"}
    D -- Yes --> E["Flip last row of Vᵀ<br/>(prevent reflection)"]
    D -- No --> F["Keep Vᵀ unchanged"]
    E --> G["Optimal rotation<br/>R* = U · Vᵀ"]
    F --> G
    G --> H["Apply transform<br/>P_aligned = R* · P̄ + mean(Q)"]
```

**Step 1 — Centering:** Both point sets are translated so that their centroids lie at the origin. The translation vectors are `translation_geom = geom.mean(0)` and `translation_ref_geom = ref_geom.mean(0)`. Centering decouples the rotational and translational components of the alignment, reducing the problem to a pure rotation.

**Step 2 — Cross-covariance and SVD:** The 3×3 cross-covariance matrix `R = (P − P̄)ᵀ · (Q − Q̄)` encodes the rotational relationship between the two point sets. Its singular value decomposition `R = U · S · Vᵀ` factorizes this relationship into orthogonal matrices U and V that span the rotational degrees of freedom.

**Step 3 — Reflection handling:** If `det(U · Vᵀ) < 0`, the decomposition has produced an improper rotation (a reflection). The algorithm corrects this by negating the last row of Vᵀ, ensuring the resulting rotation is proper (det = +1). Without this correction, pathological input geometries could produce mirrored coordinates.

**Step 4 — Transform application:** The `align` function assembles the full affine transform. The mobile structure is centered (`mobile_pos - pre_trans`), rotated via Einstein summation (`jnp.einsum("ij,bj", rot, ...)`), then translated to the reference centroid (`+ post_trans`). The einsum notation efficiently applies the 3×3 rotation matrix to every atom in the structure in a single vectorized operation.

```python
def align(mobile_pos, ref_pos, mobile_indices, ref_indices):
    l_bb, r_bb = ref_pos[ref_indices], mobile_pos[mobile_indices]
    rot, pre_trans, post_trans = affine_alignment(r_bb, l_bb)
    mobile_pos_aligned = jnp.einsum("ij,bj", rot, mobile_pos - pre_trans) + post_trans
    return mobile_pos_aligned
```

Sources: [join_fragments.py](scripts/join_fragments.py#L35-L50), [join_fragments.py](scripts/join_fragments.py#L52-L57)

## Clash Detection: Steric Violation Filtering

After alignment, the merged structure may contain atoms that were pushed into physically impossible proximity — a **steric clash**. The `check_interactions` function detects these violations through exhaustive pairwise distance computation:

```python
def check_interactions(xyz, bonds=None, cutoff=0.1):
    distances = jnp.sqrt(((xyz[:, None] - xyz[None, :]) ** 2).sum(-1))
    mask = distances < cutoff
    mask = mask.at[tuple(bonds.T)].set(False)   # exclude bonded pairs
    mask = jnp.triu(mask, k=1)                   # upper triangle only (j > i)
    return mask
```

The algorithm operates in three passes:

| Pass | Operation | Rationale |
|------|-----------|-----------|
| **Distance matrix** | `√(Σ(xᵢ - xⱼ)²)` for all pairs | Complete pairwise distance field |
| **Bond exclusion** | Set `mask[bonded_pairs] = False` | Bonded atoms are expected to be close; they must not trigger violations |
| **Upper triangle** | `jnp.triu(mask, k=1)` | Each pair appears once; avoids double-counting and excludes self-distances (k=1 skips diagonal) |

The **cutoff of 0.1 nm (1.0 Å)** is well below the van der Waals radii of any atom pair. At this threshold, a flagged interaction does not represent a marginal steric overlap — it signals a catastrophic geometric violation where two non-bonded atoms occupy nearly the same point in space. Such configurations are physically impossible and must be rejected.

The bond table is derived from MDTraj's `top.create_standard_bonds()`, which generates standard covalent bonds for the merged topology. This ensures that legitimate 1–2 and 1–3 bonded interactions (which naturally have short distances) are never misidentified as clashes.

Sources: [join_fragments.py](scripts/join_fragments.py#L60-L68), [join_fragments.py](scripts/join_fragments.py#L88-L97)

## The Combined Validation Gate

The `_join_fragments` function unifies alignment and clash detection into a single vectorized validation pipeline. For each candidate pair of fragment structures drawn from the left and right ensembles, it performs four operations in sequence:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Sample random<br/>structure indices"] --> B["Align right fragment<br/>onto left fragment"]
    B --> C["Compute RMSD<br/>over overlap atoms"]
    C --> D["Check steric<br/>clashes"]
    D --> E{"RMSD < 0.6 Å<br/>AND<br/>no clashes?"}
    E -- Pass --> F["Accept joined<br/>conformation"]
    E -- Fail --> G["Reject<br/>conformation"]
```

```python
def align_and_validate(rpos, lpos, r_indices, l_indices):
    rpos_aligned = align(rpos, lpos, r_indices, l_indices)
    rmsd = compute_rmsd(rpos_aligned[r_indices], lpos[l_indices])
    pos = jnp.concatenate([lpos[:lhs], rpos_aligned[rhs:]])
    mask = check_interactions(pos, bonds)
    no_clash_mask = ~mask.any()
    return pos, no_clash_mask, rmsd
```

**Alignment** produces the optimally superimposed right fragment. **RMSD** is computed over the 4 peptide-bond anchor atoms to quantify residual misalignment — even after optimal rotation, the two fragments' overlap atoms will not perfectly coincide because they come from different database structures with different backbone conformations. **Structure assembly** concatenates the left fragment's atoms up to the overlap boundary (`lpos[:lhs]`) with the aligned right fragment's atoms beyond the overlap (`rpos_aligned[rhs:]`), producing the full merged coordinate array. **Clash detection** then scans this merged structure for steric violations.

The final acceptance mask requires **both** criteria to be satisfied simultaneously:

```python
mask = (rmsds < 0.06) & no_clash_mask  # 0.6 Angstrom RMSD threshold
```

| Criterion | Threshold | Physical Interpretation |
|-----------|-----------|------------------------|
| Overlap RMSD | < 0.06 nm (0.6 Å) | Backbone atoms at the junction agree to sub-Ångström precision |
| No steric clash | 0 non-bonded pairs < 0.1 nm | No catastrophic atomic overlaps exist in the merged structure |

The 0.6 Å RMSD threshold is exceptionally stringent. For reference, the typical coordinate uncertainty in X-ray crystallography at 2.0 Å resolution is ~0.2 Å, and NMR ensemble members routinely differ by 1–2 Å RMSD on local backbone segments. The tight threshold ensures that only joins where the two fragments are nearly indistinguishable in the overlap region are accepted, preserving local structural integrity at the junction.

> [!TIP]
> When no candidate pairs pass both filters after 5 retry attempts with different random samples, the algorithm falls back to accepting a single random join (with a logged warning). This prevents pipeline failure for sequences where the fragment database provides only poorly overlapping structures.

Sources: [join_fragments.py](scripts/join_fragments.py#L100-L127)

## JAX Vectorization: Batch Validation at Scale

The validation gate is executed not once but **tens to hundreds of thousands of times** per fragment pair — the `joins_to_attempt_per_pairing` parameter defaults to 500,000. This is made feasible by JAX's `vmap`, which transforms the per-pair `align_and_validate` function into a batched operation that runs on GPU in a single compiled XLA kernel:

```python
pos, no_clash_mask, rmsds = vmap(align_and_validate, in_axes=(0, 0, None, None))(
    rpos, lpos, r_indices, l_indices
)
```

The `in_axes=(0, 0, None, None)` specification indicates that `rpos` and `lpos` are batched along their first axis (different structure samples), while `r_indices` and `l_indices` are shared constants (the same overlap atoms are used for all pairs). This avoids redundant index computation and reduces memory traffic.

To prevent GPU out-of-memory errors on large merged structures, the `jit_chunked_vmap` function decomposes the full batch into chunks sized according to an estimated memory budget:

```python
batch_size = lambda nres, target=10: target / (1e-5 * (nres**2))  # target in GB
```

The O(n²) scaling accounts for the pairwise distance matrix in `check_interactions`, which dominates memory usage. Each chunk is processed via `jax.lax.scan`, and the results are reassembled into a flat output array. This ensures that the algorithm scales to arbitrarily long sequences without exceeding available GPU memory.

Sources: [join_fragments.py](scripts/join_fragments.py#L123-L126), [join_fragments.py](scripts/join_fragments.py#L140-L156), [join_fragments.py](scripts/join_fragments.py#L158-L197)

## Probability-Weighted Sampling and Retry Logic

Not all structure candidates in a fragment ensemble are equally likely. The `join_fragments` function uses **probability-weighted random sampling** to preferentially select structures with higher statistical weight when drawing candidate pairs for joining:

```python
random_indices = tuple(
    random.choice(key, jnp.arange(len(pos)), shape=(n,), p=probs)
    for key, pos, probs in ((lkey, lpos, lprobs), (rkey, rpos, rprobs))
)
```

The probability vectors (`probs`) are derived from the frequency of each structure's source fragment in the database — structures that appear as hits in multiple database entries receive higher weight via the `get_probs` function, which computes inverse-count weights from unique value frequencies. After each successful join, the output ensemble's probabilities are set to the element-wise product of the source fragment probabilities, propagating statistical confidence through the hierarchical joining process.

If the combined RMSD + clash filter rejects all candidates in a batch, the algorithm resamples with a new PRNG key up to **5 attempts** before falling back to a single random join. This graceful degradation ensures that even sequences with sparse or low-quality database coverage produce an ensemble rather than failing entirely.

Sources: [join_fragments.py](scripts/join_fragments.py#L158-L197), [join_fragments.py](scripts/join_fragments.py#L130-L138)

## Algorithmic Complexity and Performance Profile

The computational cost of the overlap alignment and clash detection pipeline is dominated by two operations per candidate pair:

| Operation | Complexity per pair | Notes |
|-----------|-------------------|-------|
| Kabsch alignment (SVD) | O(1) | Fixed 4×3 point sets → 3×3 SVD |
| RMSD computation | O(1) | Fixed 4 overlap atoms |
| Pairwise distance matrix | O(n²) | n = total atoms in merged structure |
| Bond exclusion | O(b) | b = number of bonds |

The **O(n²) distance matrix** is the bottleneck, which is why the chunk size formula scales inversely with n². For a typical IDP of 100 residues (~1,600 heavy atoms before hydrogen inference), the distance matrix requires ~20M entries — well within GPU memory for batch sizes of ~400 candidates per chunk. The entire validation pipeline for 500,000 candidates compiles to a single XLA kernel that executes in seconds on a modern GPU.

Sources: [join_fragments.py](scripts/join_fragments.py#L60-L68), [join_fragments.py](scripts/join_fragments.py#L159-L162)

---

Understanding how fragments are geometrically validated is essential context for the next algorithm in the pipeline: [JAX Vectorized Ensemble Computation](10-jax-vectorized-ensemble-computation) covers how the full ensemble is assembled and stored after all joins have been filtered. For the upstream mechanism that produces the fragment pairs entering this algorithm, see [Hierarchical Fragment Joining](8-hierarchical-fragment-joining).

# JAX Vectorized Ensemble Computation



IDP-o leverages JAX's functional array programming model—specifically `vmap`, `jit`, and `jax.lax.scan`—to transform what would otherwise be an O(N²) serial fragment-joining loop into a **GPU-accelerated, batch-vectorized ensemble construction pipeline**. The core computational kernel aligns, validates, and filters thousands of candidate fragment joins per pairing in a single compiled XLA graph, eliminating Python-level loop overhead and achieving throughput on the order of hundreds of thousands of join attempts per second. This page dissects the three JAX kernels that power the ensemble builder: the **SVD alignment kernel**, the **vectorized clash-detection kernel**, and the **memory-adaptive chunked vmap scheduler**.

Sources: [join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L1-L348), [extract_structures_from_foldcomp_database.py](/scripts/extract_structures_from_foldcomp_database.py#L1-L326)

## GPU Memory Reservation and Runtime Configuration

Before any JAX computation begins, the runtime is configured to reserve **96% of available GPU memory** for the XLA compiler via the `XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION` environment variable. This aggressive allocation ensures that the large batch tensors produced during vectorized joining—particularly the N×N distance matrices in clash detection—can be resident in GPU memory without triggering on-demand allocation stalls. The Docker image builds on `nvcr.io/nvidia/jax:24.10-py3`, which ships the JAX/XLA runtime with CUDA 12 support and the `nerfax` library for internal-coordinate reconstruction and hydrogen inference.

```python
os.environ["XLA_PYTHON_CLIENT_MEM_FRACTION"] = ".96"
```

After the hierarchical ensemble build completes, the main entry point performs an explicit cleanup of live XLA buffers to release GPU memory before writing the final trajectory to disk:

```python
backend = jax.lib.xla_bridge.get_backend()
for buf in backend.live_buffers():
    buf.delete()
```

Sources: [join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L22-L22), [join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L289-L292)

## The SVD Alignment Kernel

The alignment kernel implements the **Kabsch algorithm** in pure `jnp` operations, making it fully differentiable and `vmap`-compatible. Given a mobile geometry and a reference geometry (both as N×3 coordinate arrays), the kernel computes the optimal rigid-body rotation that minimizes RMSD between the two point sets.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Mobile Geometry (N×3)"] --> B["Center both point sets"]
    C["Reference Geometry (N×3)"] --> B
    B --> D["Cross-covariance: R = (geom - t_geom)ᵀ · (ref - t_ref)"]
    D --> E["SVD: R = U·S·Vᵀ"]
    E --> F{"det(U·Vᵀ) < 0?"}
    F -- Yes --> G["Flip last row of Vᵀ"]
    F -- No --> H["Keep Vᵀ"]
    G --> I["Rotation = U · Vᵀ"]
    H --> I
    I --> J["Return (rotation, pre_translation, post_translation)"]
```

The implementation uses `jnp.linalg.svd` with `full_matrices=False` for the thin decomposition, then applies a **reflection correction**: if the determinant of U·Vᵀ is negative, the last row of Vᵀ is negated to ensure a proper rotation (det = +1) rather than an improper reflection. This correction is implemented as a `jnp.where` conditional, which remains traceable under `jit` compilation.

The `align` function then applies the affine transformation to the full mobile structure (not just the overlap residues) using `jnp.einsum("ij,bj", rot, mobile_pos - pre_trans) + post_trans`, where the Einstein summation convention efficiently expresses the batch rotation application.

| Component | JAX Operation | Shape | Purpose |
|-----------|--------------|-------|---------|
| Cross-covariance | `jnp.dot((geom - t).T, (ref - t))` | (3, 3) | Optimal rotation target |
| Thin SVD | `jnp.linalg.svd(R, full_matrices=False)` | U,S,Vᵀ each (3,3) | Decompose rotation |
| Reflection fix | `jnp.where(det < 0, Vt.at[-1].multiply(-1), Vt)` | (3, 3) | Ensure proper rotation |
| Batch rotation | `jnp.einsum("ij,bj", rot, pos)` | (N, 3) | Apply to all atoms |

Sources: [join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L38-L57)

## Vectorized Clash Detection

The `check_interactions` function computes a full pairwise distance matrix and identifies steric clashes—atoms closer than a configurable cutoff distance (default 0.1 nm = 1.0 Å) that are not connected by a covalent bond. This is the most memory-intensive operation in the join pipeline because it materializes an N×N distance matrix.

```python
distances = jnp.sqrt(((xyz[:, None] - xyz[None, :]) ** 2).sum(-1))
mask = distances < cutoff
mask = mask.at[tuple(bonds.T)].set(False)   # exclude bonded pairs
mask = jnp.triu(mask, k=1)                   # upper triangle only (j > i)
```

The broadcasting `xyz[:, None] - xyz[None, :]` creates the pairwise difference tensor without an explicit Python loop. Bonded atom pairs are explicitly excluded by indexing into the mask with the bond table transposed as a tuple of index arrays. The `jnp.triu` with `k=1` ensures each violation is counted exactly once. The resulting boolean mask is then reduced with `.any()` in the join kernel to produce a single `no_clash_mask` per candidate join.

> [!TIP]
> The N×N distance matrix is the primary memory bottleneck. The `batch_size` function in `join_fragments` dynamically computes the chunk size as `target_GB / (1e-5 × nres²)`, where `target_GB = 10` GB. For a 100-residue protein, this yields a chunk size of ~100, keeping peak memory within the 96% GPU reservation.

Sources: [join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L60-L69)

## The Vectorized Join Kernel: `_join_fragments`

The `_join_fragments` function is the **inner computational loop** of the ensemble builder. It receives pairs of randomly sampled left and right fragment conformations and, for each pair, performs overlap alignment, RMSD computation, clash checking, and produces a merged coordinate array—all within a single `vmap`-decorated function.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph "Per-pair (vmap axis)"
        A["Sample L_pos, R_pos"] --> B["Extract overlap indices"]
        B --> C["Align R to L on overlap"]
        C --> D["Compute overlap RMSD"]
        D --> E["Concatenate: L[:lhs] ++ R_aligned[rhs:]"]
        E --> F["Clash detection on merged structure"]
        F --> G["Mask = (RMSD < 0.06 Å) AND no_clash"]
    end
```

The key architectural insight is that `vmap` is applied **only over the batch dimension** of the sampled conformations, while the overlap indices (`l_indices`, `r_indices`) are broadcast as `None` in `in_axes`. This means the SVD alignment and clash detection are compiled once for a specific overlap pattern and reused across all N candidates in the batch:

```python
pos, no_clash_mask, rmsds = vmap(align_and_validate, in_axes=(0, 0, None, None))(
    rpos, lpos, r_indices, l_indices
)
mask = (rmsds < 0.06) & no_clash_mask   # 0.6 Å overlap RMSD threshold
```

The **acceptance mask** combines two criteria: the overlap RMSD must be below 0.06 nm (0.6 Å), and the merged structure must have no steric clashes. This dual filter ensures both geometric consistency at the join seam and physical plausibility of the full conformation.

Sources: [join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L96-L123)

## Memory-Adaptive Chunked vmap: `jit_chunked_vmap`

Direct `vmap` over hundreds of thousands of candidates would exceed GPU memory for the N×N distance matrices. The `jit_chunked_vmap` scheduler solves this by **splitting the batch into memory-safe chunks** and iterating over them using `jax.lax.scan`, which maintains a fixed memory footprint per iteration.

```python
def jit_chunked_vmap(f, args, chunk_size):
    lengths = jax.tree.flatten(jax.tree.map(lambda x: jnp.shape(x)[0], args))[0]
    assert len(set(lengths)) == 1

    def _body(_, args):
        return (None, f(*args))

    _, outputs = jax.lax.scan(
        _body,
        init=None,
        xs=jax.tree.map(lambda x: x.reshape((-1, chunk_size) + x.shape[1:]), args),
    )
    return jax.tree.map(lambda x: x.reshape((-1,) + x.shape[2:]), outputs)
```

The function operates in three phases: **(1)** reshape all input pytrees from `(N, ...)` to `(N/chunk_size, chunk_size, ...)`, **(2)** scan over the leading dimension applying `f` to each chunk (where `f` itself contains the `vmap` over the chunk's batch dimension), and **(3)** reshape the output back to `(N, ...)`. Because `jax.lax.scan` reuses the same XLA buffer across iterations, peak memory is bounded by the cost of a single chunk rather than the full batch.

| Parameter | Formula | Example (100 residues) |
|-----------|---------|----------------------|
| Target memory | 10 GB | 10 GB |
| Chunk size | `10 / (1e-5 × nres²)` | 100 |
| Total attempts | Rounded up to multiple of chunk_size | 500,000 → 500,000 |
| Peak memory per chunk | O(chunk_size × nres²) | ~10 GB |

Sources: [join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L132-L144), [join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L150-L152)

## Probabilistic Sampling and Join Orchestration

The `join_fragments` function implements an **importance-weighted stochastic join**. Rather than exhaustively testing all pairs of left and right conformations (which would be O(M²) where M is the number of conformations per fragment), it samples indices from each fragment's conformation pool using `jax.random.choice` with per-structure probability weights:

```python
random_indices = tuple(
    random.choice(key, jnp.arange(len(pos)), shape=(n,), p=probs)
    for key, pos, probs in ((lkey, lpos, lprobs), (rkey, rpos, rprobs))
)
```

The probability weights (`probs`) are computed by the `get_probs` function, which assigns **inverse-frequency weights** based on how many times each structure's source indices appear in the pool. This deduplicates overrepresented conformations that arise from multiple fragment sources mapping to the same Foldcomp entry:

```python
def get_probs(x):
    _, indices, counts = jnp.unique(x, return_counts=True, return_inverse=True, size=x.shape[0])
    probs = (1 / counts)[indices]
    return probs
```

When joining two fragments, the output probabilities are the **element-wise product** of the left and right probability arrays, computed via `jax.tree.map(jnp.multiply, *map(get_probs, sources))`. This multiplicative combination reflects the independence assumption between fragment conformation selections.

If no joins pass the acceptance mask after sampling, the function **retries up to 5 times** with new random keys, issuing a warning on each attempt. After 5 failures, it falls back to selecting a single random structure, ensuring the pipeline always produces output rather than crashing.

Sources: [join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L147-L192), [join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L126-L129)

## Hierarchical Ensemble Assembly: `build_ensemble`

The `build_ensemble` function orchestrates the **tree-reduction pattern** for combining N fragments into a single ensemble. Rather than joining fragments linearly (which would accumulate alignment errors), it decomposes N into a sum of powers of two and performs pairwise joins in a hierarchical tree:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph "Power-of-2 decomposition for N=7"
        F1["f₁"] --> J1["Join"]
        F2["f₂"] --> J1
        F3["f₃"] --> J2["Join"]
        F4["f₄"] --> J2
        F5["f₅"] --> J3["Join"]
        F6["f₆"] --> J3
        J1 --> J4["Join"]
        J2 --> J4
        J3 --> J5["Join (linear)"]
        F7["f₇"] --> J5
        J4 --> J6["Join (linear)"]
        J5 --> J6
    end
```

The decomposition uses `np.unpackbits` on a 32-bit unsigned integer representation of the fragment count to extract the binary representation, then `2 ** np.arange(16)[::-1]` masked by the bit array to yield the power-of-two segments. For N=7, this produces segments [4, 2, 1], which are joined in order: first the 4-fragment block (two levels of pairwise joining), then the 2-fragment block (one level), then the 1-fragment singleton.

After all power-of-two subsets are independently assembled, they are **linearly combined** in a final sequential pass. This hybrid strategy minimizes the depth of the join tree (reducing error propagation) while handling arbitrary fragment counts without padding.

**Memory management** is integrated into the hierarchy: after each level of joining completes (i.e., when `i > 1`), the intermediate fragment data from two levels prior is explicitly deleted from the `data` dictionary using `jax.tree.map` to call `.delete()` on any `jax.Array` objects, freeing GPU memory for the next level of joins.

Sources: [join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L195-L249)

## JAX in Structure Reconstruction (CPU Mode)

While the join pipeline runs on GPU, the structure reconstruction stage in `extract_structures_from_foldcomp_database.py` explicitly forces **CPU execution** via `os.environ["JAX_PLATFORMS"] = "cpu"`. This separation exists because the reconstruction kernel (`reconstruct_from_internal_coordinates_pure_sequential`) is inherently sequential—each residue's position depends on the preceding residue's computed coordinates—and does not benefit from GPU parallelism for individual structures.

Instead, JAX's `vmap` is applied **across the batch dimension** to reconstruct multiple structures in parallel:

```python
def build_parallel_reconstruct_fn(sequence):
    return build_reconstruct_fn(sequence, reconstruct_fn=vmap(reconstruct, in_axes=(0, 0, None, 0)))
```

The `in_axes=(0, 0, None, 0)` specification vectorizes over the discretizer parameters, angle/torsion arrays, and sidechain angles, while keeping the amino acid sequence (axis `None`) constant—since all structures in a fragment ensemble share the same sequence. The `@jit` decorator on the inner function, combined with `jax.ensure_compile_time_eval()`, locks the amino acid indices as compile-time constants, enabling the XLA compiler to unroll sidechain reconstruction logic specific to that sequence. This specialization can yield **~2000× speedup** compared to the non-specialized path.

Sources: [extract_structures_from_foldcomp_database.py](/scripts/extract_structures_from_foldcomp_database.py#L17-L17), [extract_structures_from_foldcomp_database.py](/scripts/extract_structures_from_foldcomp_database.py#L189-L206)

## JAX Pattern Summary

The following table consolidates all JAX patterns used across the ensemble computation pipeline, their locations, and their specific roles:

| JAX Pattern | Location | Role | Hardware |
|-------------|----------|------|----------|
| `vmap` (batch alignment) | `join_fragments.py#L121` | Vectorize alignment+validation over N candidate pairs | GPU |
| `vmap` (batch reconstruction) | `extract_structures...py#L206` | Vectorize structure reconstruction over M structures | CPU |
| `jax.lax.scan` (chunked vmap) | `join_fragments.py#L139` | Memory-bounded iteration over chunked batches | GPU |
| `jnp.linalg.svd` | `join_fragments.py#L43` | Kabsch alignment rotation | GPU |
| `jnp.einsum` | `join_fragments.py#L56` | Batch rotation application | GPU |
| `random.choice` | `join_fragments.py#L166` | Importance-weighted stochastic sampling | GPU |
| `jax.tree.map` | `join_fragments.py#L222,L231` | Pytree manipulation for probability weights and cleanup | GPU |
| `@jit` + `ensure_compile_time_eval` | `extract_structures...py#L192-L199` | Compile-time sequence specialization | CPU |
| `jnp.where` (reflection fix) | `join_fragments.py#L44-L48` | Traceable conditional for proper rotation | GPU |

> [!TIP]
> The dual-hardware strategy (GPU for joins, CPU for reconstruction) is not accidental. The join kernel's N×N distance matrix and batch SVD decompositions are highly parallelizable and benefit enormously from GPU throughput. The reconstruction kernel's sequential dependency chain (residue i+1 depends on residue i) makes it latency-bound on GPU but bandwidth-efficient on CPU, where XLA's CPU backend avoids PCIe transfer overhead for the ~1 GB Foldcomp database reads.

Sources: [join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L28-L33), [join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L38-L72), [extract_structures_from_foldcomp_database.py](/scripts/extract_structures_from_foldcomp_database.py#L28-L29)

## Computational Complexity and Scaling

The computational cost of the ensemble build is dominated by the clash detection step within each chunked vmap iteration. For a single join attempt on a structure with `nres` residues:

- **Alignment**: O(nres) — SVD on a 3×3 matrix is constant; einsum is O(nres)
- **Distance matrix**: O(nres²) — pairwise broadcasting creates nres×nres×3 tensor
- **Clash mask**: O(nres²) — comparison + bond exclusion + triu

For `N` total join attempts with chunk size `C`, the total cost is O(N/C × C × nres²) = O(N × nres²). The chunk size `C = 10 / (1e-5 × nres²)` is chosen precisely so that each chunk's O(C × nres²) memory footprint fits within ~10 GB, making the algorithm **memory-scalable**: larger proteins automatically reduce the chunk size to stay within the GPU memory budget.

| Residues | Chunk Size | Memory per Chunk | Attempts | Total Cost |
|----------|-----------|-----------------|----------|------------|
| 50 | 400 | ~10 GB | 500K | O(500K × 2500) |
| 100 | 100 | ~10 GB | 500K | O(500K × 10000) |
| 200 | 25 | ~10 GB | 500K | O(500K × 40000) |
| 500 | 4 | ~10 GB | 500K | O(500K × 250000) |

Sources: [join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L150-L152), [join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L60-L69)

## Relationship to Adjacent Pipeline Stages

The JAX vectorized ensemble computation sits at the convergence point of two upstream data flows and feeds one downstream consumer. The [Overlap Alignment and Clash Detection](9-overlap-alignment-and-clash-detection) page covers the mathematical foundations of the SVD alignment and distance-based clash criteria that this JAX kernel implements. The [Structure Reconstruction from Foldcomp](7-structure-reconstruction-from-foldcomp) page describes the CPU-side `vmap`-batched reconstruction that produces the fragment coordinate pools consumed by the join kernel. The [Hierarchical Fragment Joining](8-hierarchical-fragment-joining) page explains the tree-reduction strategy that orchestrates when and how the JAX kernel is invoked across the fragment hierarchy.

For the complete pipeline configuration options that control the JAX kernel's behavior (chunk sizes, attempt counts, ensemble sizes), see [Command-Line Configuration Reference](13-command-line-configuration-reference).

# Batch Dataset Generation



IDP-o's batch dataset generation system transforms a collection of protein sequences—provided as either a CSV or FASTA file—into a complete dataset of structural ensembles. The orchestrator script `generate_dataset.py` iterates over every sequence in the input, dispatching each one to the full three-stage pipeline (GPU-accelerated search → structure reconstruction → fragment joining) via a subprocess call to `build_ensemble.py`. This design separates **batch-level concerns** (input parsing, deduplication, parallelization, error resilience) from **sequence-level concerns** (the actual ensemble computation), enabling scalable dataset generation across thousands of intrinsically disordered proteins.

Sources: [generate_dataset.py](/generate_dataset.py#L1-L126), [scripts/build_ensemble.py](/scripts/build_ensemble.py#L1-L167)

## Batch Orchestrator Architecture

The batch system is driven entirely by `generate_dataset.py`, which acts as a lightweight coordinator. It does not import the pipeline stages directly—instead, it invokes `build_ensemble.py` as a subprocess via `subprocess.check_call`. This architectural choice provides **process isolation**: a crash or GPU memory leak in one ensemble computation cannot corrupt the state of the orchestrator or subsequent sequences.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Input File<br/>(.csv or .fasta)"] --> B["Parse & Deduplicate"]
    B --> C{"--shuffle?"}
    C -- Yes --> D["Randomize Row Order"]
    C -- No --> E["Preserve Input Order"]
    D --> F["Iterate Sequences"]
    E --> F
    F --> G["Spawn build_ensemble.py<br/>subprocess per sequence"]
    G --> H{"Success?"}
    H -- Yes --> I["Increment Counter"]
    H -- No --> J["Log Error to .txt File"]
    I --> K{"More Sequences?"}
    J --> K
    K -- Yes --> F
    K -- No --> L["Report Total Ensembles Generated"]
```

The orchestrator reads the input file, deduplicates rows, optionally shuffles the processing order, then loops through each sequence dispatching it to `build_ensemble.py`. On failure, it captures the full traceback and writes it to a companion `.txt` file alongside the expected output path, allowing the batch to continue uninterrupted.

Sources: [generate_dataset.py](/generate_dataset.py#L67-L125)

## Input Format Handling

The batch generator accepts two input formats, each with specific column-mapping semantics controlled by the `--column_names` flag:

| Format | Detection Rule | Parsing Method | Required Columns |
|--------|---------------|----------------|-----------------|
| **FASTA** (`.fasta`) | Filename ends with `.fasta` | Line-by-line: header stripped of `>` prefix → sequence on next line | Implicit: `>name` then `sequence` |
| **CSV** (`.csv`) | Filename ends with `.csv` | `pandas.read_csv` with `usecols` for selective loading | Configurable via `--column_names` |

The `--column_names` parameter defaults to `seq_name,fasta` and is split on the comma to identify the sequence identifier column and the amino acid sequence column. For FASTA files, these column names are assigned to the internally constructed DataFrame. For CSV files, only the two specified columns are loaded into memory, minimizing I/O for wide tables.

**Deduplication** is performed on both columns independently. If duplicate sequence names or duplicate FASTA strings are detected, a warning is logged and duplicates are dropped with `pandas.drop_duplicates`, retaining only the first occurrence.

Sources: [generate_dataset.py](/generate_dataset.py#L67-L87)

## Subprocess Dispatch and Error Resilience

For each sequence row, the orchestrator constructs a command list that invokes `build_ensemble.py` with the following arguments:

| Argument | Value Source | Description |
|----------|-------------|-------------|
| `--sequence` | `row[fasta]` | The amino acid sequence string |
| `--outpath` | `{outfolder}/{seq_name}.{format}` | Output file path derived from sequence name and format |
| `--scratch_folder` | `/tmp/tmp-{seq_name}` | Isolated scratch directory per sequence |
| `--max_structures_in_ensemble` | CLI argument `--max_structures_in_ensemble` | Frames to retain in final ensemble |
| `--overwrite` | CLI flag | Passed through if specified |

> [!TIP]
> Each sequence receives an **isolated scratch directory** under `/tmp/tmp-{seq_name}`. This prevents intermediate files (fragment ensembles, byte-start pickles) from colliding when running multiple batch processes concurrently against the same input file.

When a subprocess fails, the exception is caught, the full traceback is formatted, and both the command that was attempted and the error are written to `{seq_name}.txt` in the output folder. The batch then proceeds to the next sequence. This **fail-open** strategy ensures that a single problematic sequence (e.g., one with non-standard amino acids) does not halt dataset generation for the remaining entries.

Sources: [generate_dataset.py](/generate_dataset.py#L97-L125)

## Shuffle-Based Parallelization

The `--shuffle` flag randomizes the processing order of sequences using `pandas.sample(frac=1)`. This is not merely cosmetic—it is the **primary mechanism for distributed parallelization**. Since each sequence is processed independently (no shared mutable state between iterations), multiple workers can independently run `generate_dataset.py` against the **same input file** with `--shuffle` enabled. By statistical expectation, each worker will process a different random subset first, naturally distributing the workload without any central coordinator or queue system.

In practice, you would partition work by launching N containers or processes, each reading the same input file with `--shuffle`. The `--overwrite` flag should be omitted so that completed ensembles (whose output files already exist) are skipped by `build_ensemble.py`, providing implicit **idempotent checkpointing**.

Sources: [generate_dataset.py](/generate_dataset.py#L94-L96), [scripts/build_ensemble.py](/scripts/build_ensemble.py#L40-L45)

## Per-Sequence Pipeline Integration

Each subprocess invocation triggers the full three-stage pipeline inside `build_ensemble.py`, which chains the three core scripts as module-level function calls:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["fasta_search_in_foldcomp_database<br/>.main()"] -->|"byte_starts.pkl"| B["extract_structures_from_foldcomp_database<br/>.main()"]
    B -->|"fragment_ensembles/*.h5"| C["join_fragments<br/>.main()"]
    C --> D["Final Ensemble<br/>(.h5 / .xtc / .pdb / .dcd)"]
```

| Stage | Script | Input | Output | Key Parameters Passed |
|-------|--------|-------|--------|----------------------|
| **1. Search** | `fasta_search_in_foldcomp_database` | Sequence, foldcomp FASTA | `byte_starts.pkl` | `sequence`, `foldcomp_fasta`, `reduction_factor` |
| **2. Reconstruct** | `extract_structures_from_foldcomp_database` | Foldcomp DB, byte starts | Fragment `.h5` files | `foldcomp_fasta`, `foldcomp_db`, `n_max_structures_per_fragment`, `exclude_cis_omega` |
| **3. Join** | `join_fragments` | Fragment `.h5` files | Final ensemble | `joins_to_attempt_per_pairing`, `max_structures_in_ensemble`, `rmsd_sort` |

The batch orchestrator only exposes `--max_structures_in_ensemble` and `--overwrite` to the subprocess; all other pipeline parameters (`foldcomp_fasta`, `foldcomp_db`, `reduction_factor`, `n_max_structures_per_fragment`, `joins_to_attempt_per_pairing`, `exclude_cis_omega`, `rmsd_sort`) fall back to their defaults inside `build_ensemble.py`. This keeps the batch interface simple while relying on sensible per-sequence defaults.

Sources: [scripts/build_ensemble.py](/scripts/build_ensemble.py#L60-L80), [scripts/build_ensemble.py](/scripts/build_ensemble.py#L91-L142)

## Output File Organization

The batch generator writes one ensemble file per input sequence into the specified `--outfolder` directory. The naming convention is `{sequence_name}.{format}`, where the format extension is determined by the `--format` flag:

| Format | Extension | Trajectory Topology File | Notes |
|--------|-----------|--------------------------|-------|
| **HDF5** | `.h5` | Embedded | Native MDTraj format; most efficient for I/O |
| **XTC** | `.xtc` | Companion `.pdb` | GROMACS compressed format; `.pdb` written for first frame |
| **DCD** | `.dcd` | Companion `.pdb` | CHARMM format; `.pdb` written for first frame |
| **PDB** | `.pdb` | N/A | Single-frame; only last conformation retained |
| **PDB.GZ** | `.pdb.gz` | N/A | Gzip-compressed PDB |

> [!TIP]
> For trajectory formats (`.xtc`, `.dcd`), `join_fragments.py` automatically writes a companion `.pdb` file containing the topology from the first frame. This is required because these binary formats store only coordinates—the `.pdb` provides the atom names, residue information, and bond connectivity needed by downstream tools.

Failed sequences produce a `.txt` error log instead of a structure file, making it straightforward to identify and retry failed entries.

Sources: [generate_dataset.py](/generate_dataset.py#L100-L124), [scripts/join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L317-L319)

## Safety Guard and Dry-Run Mode

When `--max_structures_in_ensemble` is omitted or set to `0` (the default), the orchestrator loads and deduplicates the input file but **does not spawn any subprocesses**. Instead, it logs a warning: `"set '--max_structures_in_ensemble' to actually generate the ensembles"`. This serves as a **safety guard** against accidental full-dataset runs (which could take hours or days) and doubles as a **dry-run/validation mode**—you can confirm that your input file parses correctly and check the deduplication warnings before committing to the full computation.

Sources: [generate_dataset.py](/generate_dataset.py#L91-L93)

## CLI Reference Summary

The following table summarizes all arguments accepted by `generate_dataset.py`:

| Argument | Short | Type | Default | Required | Description |
|----------|-------|------|---------|----------|-------------|
| `--input` | `-i` | `str` | — | **Yes** | Path to input CSV or FASTA file |
| `--outfolder` | `-o` | `str` | `./ensembles` | No | Output directory for ensemble files |
| `--max_structures_in_ensemble` | `-n` | `int` | `0` | No | Frames per ensemble; `0` = dry run |
| `--fragments_overlap` | — | `int` | `1` | No | Overlapping residues between fragments |
| `--column_names` | — | `str` | `seq_name,fasta` | No | Column names in CSV (comma-separated) |
| `--shuffle` | — | flag | `False` | No | Randomize processing order for parallelization |
| `--format` | — | `str` | `xtc` | No | Output format: `h5`, `xtc`, `pdb`, `pdb.gz`, `dcd` |
| `--overwrite` | — | flag | `False` | No | Overwrite existing ensemble files |

Sources: [generate_dataset.py](/generate_dataset.py#L24-L59)

## Typical Usage Patterns

**Single-machine batch generation** from a CSV file with 500 sequences:

```bash
docker run -v $(pwd):/data --gpus 1 idp-o \
  python /IDP-o/generate_dataset.py \
    --input /data/sequences.csv \
    --outfolder /data/ensembles \
    --max_structures_in_ensemble 100 \
    --format h5
```

**Distributed parallelization** across 4 GPUs on separate machines, all reading the same input:

```bash
# On each machine (runs 1-4):
docker run -v $(pwd):/data --gpus 1 idp-o \
  python /IDP-o/generate_dataset.py \
    --input /data/sequences.csv \
    --outfolder /data/ensembles \
    --max_structures_in_ensemble 100 \
    --shuffle \
    --format xtc
```

Each worker independently shuffles and processes sequences; already-completed ensembles are skipped due to the absence of `--overwrite`, providing natural work-stealing behavior.

**Validation dry run** to check input parsing before a long batch:

```bash
python generate_dataset.py \
  --input sequences.fasta \
  --outfolder ./ensembles
# Leaves -n at default 0 → logs count and duplicates, no computation
```

Sources: [generate_dataset.py](/generate_dataset.py#L23-L59)

## Next Steps

- For the per-sequence pipeline that each batch invocation triggers, see [Architecture Overview](4-architecture-overview) and the individual pipeline stage pages: [GPU-Accelerated Sequence Search](6-gpu-accelerated-sequence-search), [Structure Reconstruction from Foldcomp](7-structure-reconstruction-from-foldcomp), and [Hierarchical Fragment Joining](8-hierarchical-fragment-joining).
- For details on the output file formats and how to consume them in downstream analyses, see [Output Formats and Downstream Use](12-output-formats-and-downstream-use).
- For the complete set of CLI arguments across all scripts (including per-sequence parameters not exposed by the batch wrapper), see [Command-Line Configuration Reference](13-command-line-configuration-reference).

# Output Formats and Downstream Use



IDP-o produces **structurally complete, multi-frame protein ensembles** — trajectory files where each frame represents one plausible conformation of an intrinsically disordered protein. The output is deliberately designed to be immediately consumable by standard molecular dynamics (MD) analysis toolkits, visualization software, and downstream simulation engines, with no post-processing required. This page details every format IDP-o can emit, the auxiliary files it generates alongside the primary output, and concrete patterns for integrating those outputs into common downstream workflows.

Sources: [generate_dataset.py](/generate_dataset.py#L1-L126), [scripts/build_ensemble.py](/scripts/build_ensemble.py#L1-L167), [scripts/join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L1-L348)

## Supported Output Formats

IDP-o supports five trajectory formats, selectable via the `--format` flag in `generate_dataset.py` or inferred from the `--outpath` extension in `build_ensemble.py`. All formats are written through **MDTraj's** I/O layer, guaranteeing byte-level compatibility with every tool that reads these standards.

| Format | Extension | Topology Storage | Compression | Best For |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **HDF5** | `.h5` | Embedded in file | Lossless | Single-file portability, Python-native analysis |
| **XTC** | `.xtc` | Companion `.pdb` | Lossy (GROMACS) | GROMACS pipelines, large trajectories |
| **PDB** | `.pdb` | Embedded per model | None | Visual inspection, small ensembles |
| **Gzipped PDB** | `.pdb.gz` | Embedded per model | gzip | Archival, reduced disk footprint |
| **DCD** | `.dcd` | Companion `.pdb` | None | CHARMM/OpenMM pipelines |

> [!TIP]
> Choose **XTC** for production-scale datasets (hundreds of sequences × hundreds of frames) — its lossy compression achieves ~3× smaller files than DCD while preserving sub-angstrom precision, and GROMACS tools read it natively. Choose **HDF5** when your downstream analysis is entirely Python-based and you want topology + coordinates in a single file with no companion artifacts.

The format is specified at the batch level in `generate_dataset.py` through the `--format` argument, which defaults to `xtc`. Each sequence in the input CSV/FASTA produces one output file named `{sequence_name}.{format}` in the output folder.

Sources: [generate_dataset.py](/generate_dataset.py#L74-L78), [scripts/join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L321-L326)

## Companion Files and Auxiliary Outputs

### Topology Sidecar for Binary Formats

Binary trajectory formats (`.xtc`, `.dcd`) store only coordinate arrays — they lack the atom names, residue identities, and bonding information needed to interpret the coordinates. IDP-o automatically writes a **companion PDB file** containing the topology from frame 0 whenever these formats are selected:

```python
t.save(outpath)
if outpath.endswith((".xtc", ".dcd")):
    t[0].save(outpath[:-3] + "pdb")
```

This produces a file pair such as `P53_TAD.xtc` + `P53_TAD.pdb`. The companion PDB is a **single-frame file** (frame 0 of the ensemble) that serves as the topology reference for all downstream tools that require separate coordinate + topology inputs.

Sources: [scripts/join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L324-L326)

### Error Logs on Generation Failure

When batch generation encounters a per-sequence failure, IDP-o does not halt the entire dataset. Instead, it writes a **plain-text error log** named `{sequence_name}.txt` alongside the expected output path, containing both the failed command and the full traceback:

```python
with open(os.path.splitext(outpath)[0] + ".txt", "w") as f:
    f.write(cmd + "\n" + error_msg + "\n")
```

This allows bulk dataset generation to continue past individual failures while preserving full diagnostic information for debugging.

Sources: [generate_dataset.py](/generate_dataset.py#L114-L116)

### Intermediate Scratch Artifacts

During ensemble construction, IDP-o writes two categories of intermediate files to the `--scratch_folder`:

| Artifact | Path Pattern | Purpose | Lifecycle |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Byte-start index** | `scratch_folder/byte_starts.pkl` | Pickled dictionary mapping each fragment to its hit positions in the Foldcomp database | Written by sequence search; consumed by structure extraction |
| **Fragment ensembles** | `scratch_folder/fragment_ensembles/{fragment}.h5` | Per-fragment HDF5 trajectories from Foldcomp reconstruction | Written by structure extraction; consumed by fragment joining |
| **Fragment ensembles (cis-excluded)** | `scratch_folder/fragment_ensembles-exclude_cis_omega/{fragment}.h5` | Same as above, but filtered for trans-ω only | Used when `--exclude_cis_omega` is active |

These intermediates are **not automatically cleaned up** after ensemble generation completes. For large batch runs, you should periodically clear the scratch directory or mount it on fast ephemeral storage.

Sources: [scripts/fasta_search_in_foldcomp_database.py](/scripts/fasta_search_in_foldcomp_database.py#L170-L173), [scripts/extract_structures_from_foldcomp_database.py](/scripts/extract_structures_from_foldcomp_database.py#L300-L305), [scripts/build_ensemble.py](/scripts/build_ensemble.py#L50-L55)

## Ensemble Structure and Completeness

### All-Atom Output with Inferred Hydrogens

The final ensemble returned by the joining pipeline undergoes a critical post-processing step: **hydrogen atom inference and insertion**. The Foldcomp database stores only heavy-atom coordinates (backbone N/CA/C/O and sidechain atoms). Before writing the output file, IDP-o calls:

```python
t = infer_and_insert_hydrogens(t)
```

This function (from the `nerfax` library) reconstructs all hydrogen positions from the heavy-atom geometry using standard bond lengths and angles, producing a **fully all-atom trajectory**. This means the output is immediately suitable for force field evaluations, NMR chemical shift predictors, and any computation that requires hydrogen positions — no external protonation step is needed.

Sources: [scripts/join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L317-L318)

### Frame Count and Selection

The number of conformations in the final ensemble is controlled by `--max_structures_in_ensemble` (default: 100 in `build_ensemble.py`). This parameter acts as a **hard ceiling** on the number of frames written to disk:

```python
t = md.Trajectory(
    data[seq]["coords"][:max_structures_in_ensemble],
    md.Topology.from_dataframe(build_mdtraj_top(seq)),
)
```

The frames are taken as the first *N* structures produced by the hierarchical joining process. When `--rmsd_sort` is enabled, these frames are **reordered** by greedy nearest-neighbor RMSD before the ceiling is applied, ensuring the selected frames form a smooth conformational path through structure space.

Sources: [scripts/join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L311-L319)

### Optional RMSD-Based Sorting

The `--rmsd_sort` flag triggers a two-step post-processing pipeline:

1. **Superposition**: All frames are aligned to frame 0 via `trajectory.superpose(trajectory, frame=0)`.
2. **Greedy RMSD ordering**: A nearest-neighbor sort through the RMSD matrix arranges frames so that consecutive frames have minimal structural deviation, producing a visually smooth trajectory when animated.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Raw Joined\nEnsemble"] --> B{"--rmsd_sort?"}
    B -- No --> C["Write Output\n(original join order)"]
    B -- Yes --> D["Superpose all\nframes to frame 0"]
    D --> E["Compute pairwise\nRMSD matrix"]
    E --> F["Greedy nearest-\nneighbor sort"]
    F --> G["Infer & insert\nhydrogens"]
    G --> H["Write Output\n(RMSD-sorted order)"]
    C --> G2["Infer & insert\nhydrogens"]
    G2 --> C2["Write Output"]
```

This sorting is primarily a **visualization aid** — it does not alter the ensemble's statistical properties, only the frame ordering.

Sources: [scripts/join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L259-L275), [scripts/join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L315-L319)

## Downstream Integration Patterns

### Loading Ensembles with MDTraj (Python)

Since IDP-o writes standard MDTraj-compatible formats, the simplest loading pattern is:

```python
import mdtraj as md

# HDF5 — topology embedded
ensemble = md.load_hdf5("P53_TAD.h5")

# XTC — topology from companion PDB
ensemble = md.load("P53_TAD.xtc", top="P53_TAD.pdb")

# DCD — topology from companion PDB
ensemble = md.load("P53_TAD.dcd", top="P53_TAD.pdb")

# Multi-model PDB
ensemble = md.load("P53_TAD.pdb")
```

All four calls return an `md.Trajectory` object with `n_frames` equal to `--max_structures_in_ensemble` and `n_atoms` including all inferred hydrogens.

### Computing Ensemble-Averaged Properties

IDP-o ensembles are designed for direct computation of IDP-relevant observables:

```python
# Radius of gyration distribution
rg = md.compute_rg(ensemble)
print(f"Rg: {rg.mean():.2f} ± {rg.std():.2f} Å")

# Per-residue RMSF (requires reference = mean structure)
rmsf = md.rmsf(ensemble, ensemble[0])

# Inter-residue distance distributions
pairs = ensemble.topology.select_pairs("resid 0", "resid 50")
dists = md.compute_distances(ensemble, pairs)
```

### Integration with GROMACS / CHARMM Pipelines

For `.xtc` output, GROMACS tools accept the file pair directly:

```bash
# Compute RMSD against a reference
gmx rms -s ref.tpr -f ensemble.xtc -o rmsd.xvg

# Cluster conformations
gmx cluster -f ensemble.xtc -s topol.tpr -method gromos -c clusters.pdb
```

For `.dcd` output, VMD and CHARMM tools consume the trajectory + PDB topology pair natively.

### NMR Chemical Shift Prediction

Because IDP-o ensembles include all hydrogen positions, they can be fed directly to chemical shift predictors such as **SPARTA+** or **ShiftX2** without any protonation step:

```python
# Export frame as PDB for SPARTA+ input
ensemble[0].save("frame_0.pdb")
# SPARTA+ reads all-atom PDB directly
```

### Batch Dataset Integration

The `generate_dataset.py` wrapper produces one ensemble per input sequence, making the output folder directly usable as a **dataset**. The naming convention `{sequence_name}.{format}` preserves the identifier from the input CSV/FASTA, enabling programmatic cross-referencing between input sequences and their ensembles. Failed sequences produce `.txt` error logs rather than ensemble files, so the presence of the ensemble file itself serves as a success indicator.

Sources: [generate_dataset.py](/generate_dataset.py#L95-L116), [scripts/join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L306-L326)

## Output Format Comparison: Decision Matrix

The following matrix summarizes trade-offs to guide format selection for specific downstream scenarios:

| Downstream Use Case | Recommended Format | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Python-only analysis (MDTraj, PyEMMA) | `.h5` | Single-file, topology embedded, fastest random frame access |
| GROMACS MD refinement | `.xtc` | Native format, lossy compression saves disk, companion PDB auto-generated |
| CHARMM/OpenMM MD refinement | `.dcd` | Native format for these engines, companion PDB auto-generated |
| Visual inspection (PyMOL, ChimeraX) | `.pdb` | Directly openable, multi-model PDB, no companion files needed |
| Long-term archival or transfer | `.pdb.gz` | Smallest standalone file, universally readable after decompression |
| Machine learning datasets | `.h5` | Efficient vectorized reads via h5py, metadata attachable |
| NMR back-calculation | `.h5` or `.xtc` | Hydrogens present; format choice depends on predictor's input API |

> [!TIP]
> When building a large-scale dataset (e.g., thousands of IDP sequences), use `.xtc` for storage efficiency and archive the companion `.pdb` files separately — they are identical for all frames of a given sequence, so you need only one per sequence. For ML training pipelines that iterate over frames repeatedly, `.h5` avoids the overhead of repeated topology parsing.

Sources: [generate_dataset.py](/generate_dataset.py#L74-L78), [scripts/join_fragments.py](/scripts/join_fragments.py#L321-L326)
